terms.definition: A segment of DNA that carries the instructions for a specific trait.
terms.function: Defines which trait a locus controls; the two alleles a Punnett square combines are both versions of the same gene.
terms.whereItIs: A defined location on a chromosome, inherited one copy from each parent.
terms.whyItMatters: A Punnett square only makes sense when both parents' alleles being crossed belong to the same gene.

terms.definition: One version of a gene; different alleles can produce different versions of the same trait.
terms.function: The letters written along a Punnett square's edges and combined inside its cells are alleles.
terms.whereItIs: One allele per gene comes from each parent; the grid's top row and left column each hold one parent's pair.
terms.whyItMatters: Without correctly identifying each parent's alleles, the whole grid produces the wrong predictions.

terms.definition: An allele whose trait shows up in the phenotype even when only one copy is present.
terms.function: Written with a capital letter (e.g. R); masks the recessive allele's trait whenever the two are paired together.
terms.whereItIs: Engraved as an uppercase letter on the parent and offspring beads in the model.
terms.whyItMatters: Dominant alleles are why a trait can appear in offspring even if only one parent visibly shows it.

terms.definition: An allele whose trait only shows up when two copies (one from each parent) are present.
terms.function: Written with a lowercase letter (e.g. r); its trait is masked whenever paired with a dominant allele, but it can still be passed on.
terms.whereItIs: Engraved as a lowercase letter on the parent and offspring beads in the model.
terms.whyItMatters: Recessive alleles explain how a trait can 'skip a generation' — two parents who don't show it can still both carry and pass it on.

terms.definition: The specific pair of alleles an organism carries for a gene, written as letters (e.g., Rr).
terms.function: Determines the phenotype according to the dominant/recessive relationship between the two alleles present.
terms.whereItIs: Read directly off each Punnett square cell — the row letter plus the column letter.
terms.whyItMatters: Genotype is the underlying code; phenotype is what you actually see — the two can differ, which is the whole point of recessive alleles.

terms.definition: The observable trait that results from an organism's genotype.
terms.function: The visible outcome produced once the dominant/recessive relationship between the two alleles in a genotype is resolved.
terms.whereItIs: Not shown directly as a letter in the grid — it's read by grouping genotypes that share the same dominant/recessive outcome.
terms.whyItMatters: Phenotype is what a Punnett square's ratio ultimately predicts and what you can actually check against real offspring.

terms.definition: Having two identical alleles for a gene, like RR or rr.
terms.function: A homozygous parent contributes the same allele no matter which of its two copies gets passed on, so all of its offspring receive that same letter.
terms.whereItIs: Both alleles in a parent's bead pair show the same letter.
terms.whyItMatters: Crossing a homozygous dominant parent (RR) with any other parent guarantees every offspring shows the dominant phenotype.

terms.definition: Having two different alleles for a gene, like Rr.
terms.function: A heterozygous parent has a 50/50 chance of passing either allele to a given offspring, which is what creates a spread of possible genotypes in the grid.
terms.whereItIs: The two alleles in a parent's bead pair show different letters.
terms.whyItMatters: Crossing two heterozygous parents (Rr x Rr) is the classic monohybrid cross that produces the 1:2:1 genotype and 3:1 phenotype ratios.

terms.definition: A grid tool that lays out all possible allele combinations from a cross between two parents.
terms.function: Systematically lists every combination two parents' alleles can produce for a gene, turning a random process into something you can see and count.
terms.whereItIs: The four-celled vertical slab at the center of the model.
terms.whyItMatters: It's the core tool geneticists and students use to predict the odds of different genotypes and traits appearing in offspring.

terms.definition: The point where each parent's two alleles for a gene line up along the grid's edges, ready to be combined into offspring genotypes.
terms.function: Supplies the raw genetic material for the cross: each parent randomly passes just one of their two alleles per gene.
terms.whereItIs: The father's two allele beads sit above the grid's top edge; the mother's two allele beads sit beside the grid's left edge.
terms.whyItMatters: This step is what makes a Punnett square accurate — it only works if you correctly identify what each parent can actually pass on.

terms.definition: The count of how many grid cells produced each possible genotype, expressed as a ratio such as 1:2:1.
terms.function: Converts the four individual grid cells into a single summary number that predicts genotype odds across many offspring.
terms.whereItIs: The left disk-tower cluster on the shelf below the grid; tower height encodes count.
terms.whyItMatters: Genotype ratios are the first checkpoint for whether a cross was set up and read correctly, before translating to visible traits.

terms.definition: The count of how many grid cells produce each visible trait, expressed as a ratio such as 3:1, after grouping genotypes that share the same trait.
terms.function: Translates genotype counts into the trait ratio you could actually observe by looking at the offspring.
terms.whereItIs: The right disk-tower cluster on the shelf below the grid, smaller than the genotype cluster.
terms.whyItMatters: Phenotype ratios are what you can actually check against real offspring — the testable prediction a Punnett square ultimately makes.
